title: Gurugram Computer Software & IT: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
A Gurugram software firm sells engineering hours and managed teams from leased offices to overseas and domestic clients; cash arrives as milestone or monthly invoices, and the gap between paying salaries and collecting from clients is the whole credit story. **The asset is people, not plant, so the bank is really financing payroll ahead of receivables.** Rating methodology flags that most Indian software revenue is earned overseas, so US spending and visa norms drive collections [9].

## Where value and cash sit
Margins depend on billing rate minus salary, bench cost and lease rent; pricing power is weak in staff-augmentation and strong only where the firm owns a product or a managed-service contract. **Receivables are the riskiest line: peer InfoBeans shows rising 90-day receivables [4], so when a proposal lands, check the ageing beyond 90 days; if it is climbing, ask for the top-five client collection history.** Capex is modest — fit-outs and laptops — but lease deposits and security are real cash outflows. AI is compressing billable hours across the US$315-billion Indian services sector [5].

## What has changed now
Local news is about offices, not software: Lodha is putting ₹1,200 crore into a 4 lakh sq ft Grade A++ project on Golf Course Road [1][2], which signals landlord confidence in Gurugram occupancy but says nothing about your borrower's cash flow. **Peer results are mixed: InfoBeans grew 22% in constant currency while profit growth trailed at 16% [4]; Sasken grew revenue 25.6% to Rs. 321 crores with EBITDA margin up 700 basis points [7]; TCS held margins despite AI spend but its stock is down 30.3% year-to-date [5].** Cognizant's Q3 beat lifted the Nifty IT index nearly 2% [6]. The rating sources are undated archived methodologies [8][9][11] — treat them as principles, not current data. Sources say little specific about Gurugram software firms, so lean on first principles and these peers.

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue product-led and managed-service firms with contracted, multi-year revenue, and GCC-support vendors serving captives already leased in Gurugram's new Grade A space [1][2].** Avoid pure onsite-staffing exporters whose revenue depends on US visas [9]. Structure as a receivable-backed line with monthly stock-and-book-debt statements, a 90-day ageing covenant and a minimum billing-rate floor. Take monthly: ageing beyond 90 days, top-five client concentration, bench percentage, and salary-to-collection gap. **Where a figure is missing, collect from customer rather than assume.**

## Early-warning signs
- Monthly ageing (monthly): 90-day-plus receivables rise two months running -> freeze fresh drawdown and reprice.
- Client concentration (quarterly): top client crosses a third of revenue -> seek assignment of that contract's receivables.
- Bench and attrition (monthly): bench rises while billing falls -> cut limit.
- Visa or onsite exposure (quarterly): onsite share of revenue grows -> ask for redeployment plan before renewal.

bench up while billing down -> reduce limit
share rising -> demand redeployment plan before renewal
